content: After removing duplicate records using both manual methods and reference software, 85 abstracts were identified for screening. Subsequently, 48 full-text articles were reviewed for potential inclusion, and 10 studies were selected for qualitative analysis. However, one of these studies, initially a conference abstract, was later published as a full paper and was excluded from the quantitative analysis. Another study did not present data in an analyzable format, leaving eight studies for further analysis. Of these, only four contributed data for both sensitivity and specificity estimates. The included studies originated from various regions: three from Europe (France, Germany, and Spain), three from Africa (Congo, Egypt, and Zambia), two from Asia (India and China), and one from Mexico. None of the studies included data from children, one study focused exclusively on women, and another included only HIV-positive patients. Overall, demographic characteristics were underreported across the studies. All studies used whole blood for dried blood spot (DBS) sample preparation, except for one study that used plasma. Diagnostic Performance Among the four studies that provided both sensitivity and specificity data, the sensitivity of HBV DNA detection in DBS ranged from 93% to 100%, while specificity ranged from 86% to 100%. A pooled bivariate analysis revealed an overall sensitivity of 96% (95% CI: 91–98) and specificity of 100% (95% CI: 55–100). In a univariate analysis of seven studies contributing to sensitivity, the pooled sensitivity was 97% (95% CI: 94–99). The agreement between binary results of HBV DNA on DBS and serum was high. Limit of Detection and Assay Thresholds No standardized guidelines exist for using HBV DNA assays on DBS. Studies tested the detection limits of both commercial and in-house assays, with serum detection limits ranging from 10 to 100 IU/mL. A threshold of 20,000 IU/mL was commonly used. Effect of Storage Conditions and Assay Type Two studies evaluated storage conditions ranging from 4°C to 37°C for up to seven days and found no decline in diagnostic accuracy. All diagnostic accuracy studies stored DBS samples at –20°C, precluding a stratified meta-analysis on storage conditions. Sensitivity was similar between in-house and commercial PCR assays (95% and 98%, respectively). Only one study used plasma instead of whole blood for DBS preparation, and its results were consistent with pooled estimates. Study Quality and Risk of Bias Most studies did not adequately report key methodological details, leading to a high risk of bias. None of the studies blinded laboratory personnel to the reference or index test results. However, all studies followed clear and consistent protocols for both reference and index tests, minimizing interpretation bias. Four studies were downgraded due to their case-control design, and five studies lacked adequate reporting on sampling or participant flow. Overall, the diagnostic accuracy studies were of low quality, with a high risk of bias. Discussion This systematic review and meta-analysis highlight the scarcity and suboptimal quality of data on the use of DBS for HBV DNA testing. The pooled meta-analysis suggests good sensitivity compared to serum and adequate specificity, albeit with high imprecision. Storage conditions did not significantly affect DBS performance. The descriptive review also demonstrated a strong correlation between HBV DNA levels in DBS and serum samples. Limitations The review had several limitations, including a small number of studies, limited quality, and small sample sizes. Only English-language literature was included, and unpublished studies were not examined. The sensitivity and specificity of certain HBV DNA thresholds, such as 2000 IU/mL (below which treatment is not recommended), could not be assessed due to the lack of individual sample data. This threshold is critical for determining inactive, immune-controlled chronic hepatitis B. Future Directions Future research should focus on larger, well-designed diagnostic accuracy studies that avoid case-control designs, test DBS under real-world storage and transport conditions, and report diagnostic accuracy for clinically relevant thresholds. A meta-analysis of individual patient-level data from published and unpublished studies could provide more robust insights. Conclusion This review underscores the potential of DBS for HBV DNA testing but highlights the need for further high-quality research to establish its diagnostic accuracy and applicability in diverse settings.
